prompt:
You maintain a running summary of a long engineering document that is being read part by part, so that a later reader can model the system in SysML v2 without seeing the earlier parts.
Update the summary with the new part. Keep, as compactly as possible: the full names of system elements, actors and items; every alias or call sign with the full name it stands for; which element produces, sends or receives which item; modes and normative requirements. At most 300 words.

Current summary:
Document: Management by Trajectory (MBT) Concept of Operations (ConOps), far-term vision for air traffic management (ATM) in the National Airspace System (NAS); interprets Trajectory Based Operations (TBO), consistent with International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) TBO Concept. Far-term: NAS and most aircraft support Aeronautical Telecommunications Network-Baseline 2 (ATN-B2). Near-term constrained by current NAS and NAS Enterprise Architecture (EA)/NextGen plans. Current NAS: automation predicts trajectories from flight plans; controllers issue open-trajectory tactical clearances; Ground Delay Programs (GDPs) and Airspace Flow Programs (AFPs) assign departure times to meet a Controlled Time of Arrival (CTA); Time Based Flow Management (TBFM); Traffic Flow Management (TFM). MBT: Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and airspace users negotiate closed four-dimensional trajectories (4DTs) for all Instrument Flight Rules (IFR) aircraft; aircraft shall follow assigned 4DTs. NAS Constraint Service publishes constraints. Traffic management automation translates traffic management initiatives (TMIs) into flight-specific trajectory constraints. Aircraft send 4DT intent. Conflicts resolved by modifying 4DT constraints. Data comm delivers 4DTs to Flight Management System (FMS); electronic flight bag (EFB) apps. Negotiating controller coordinates with traffic management coordinators (TMCs). Near-term: controllers retain separation; one active FMS Required Time of Arrival (RTA); Controller-pilot data link communications (CPDLC); System Wide Information Management (SWIM); mixed equipage; equipped participants negotiate trajectories, mostly left alone; structured airspace remains, more direct routing in low-medium density; controllers issue closed trajectories in advance via automation, not voice vectors. Far-term: capable EFBs with high-speed ground connectivity; all aircraft receive assigned trajectories digitally and fly them with known accuracy (auto-load into FMS or manual pilot loading); voice retained for immediate action; unmanned aircraft systems (UAS) tech spills over; Traffic Collision Avoidance System/Airborne Collision Avoidance System (TCAS/ACAS) evolves from UAS detect-and-avoid, converging with self-separation (Advanced Interval Management, A-IM); all IFR aircraft have coordinated tactical conflict avoidance, sending planned avoidance maneuvers to ground automation via broadband (final safety layer). TFM evolves: GDPs/AFPs control by CTA at constrained resource, not departure time.

New part:
U0076: The time horizon over which TBFM is applied will expand further into the en route environment, and TBFM will be used to address airspace constraints as well as airport capacity constraints.  Use of generic miles-in-trail (MIT) restrictions (i.e., the same restriction across many aircraft) will be eliminated.
U0077: When metering is not required, aircraft will be spaced for safety and efficiency using either time-based management or A-IM.  MBT facilitates a transition to time-based separation standards.
U0078: Whether the NAS uses distance-based or time-based separation requirements, or a combination of both, to define minimum separation standards, is inconsequential to MBT.
U0079: MBT is able to function for any type of separation requirements.  Aircraft capability to meet TOAC constraints is described using a Required Time Performance (RTP) metric that serves as a complement to existing standards used to describe Required Navigation Performance (RNP).
U0080: An aircraft’s time-based performance is denoted by RTP-Y, where Y is a variable that describes the 95% confidence interval of the expected crossing time error distribution, in seconds, regardless of its shape.
U0081: In an MBT environment, all aircraft will be certified to operate at some RTP level, including aircraft that are not equipped with automation systems that include RTA functionality.  Airspace users’ flight operations centers will develop advanced capabilities to fully participate in MBT.
U0082: Software applications and private service providers will enable non- airline flights to fully participate in MBT.  The NAS will accommodate new aircraft classes, including on-demand travel, personal mobility, UAS, space vehicle launch and return operations, airships, and loitering operations (e.g., to provide communication or ground surveillance services).
U0083: Many of these newer, emerging users are expected to have the necessary capabilities to be fully compliant with MBT. 1.6 Document Scope 1.6.1 Surface Operations This ConOps document focuses on the airborne phases of flight.
U0084: However, MBT is applicable to all phases of flight.
U0085: Although nothing in the MBT concept precludes including a surface trajectory as part of the aircraft’s 4DT, defining the surface trajectory and the aircraft following it would require new ground and aircraft automation capabilities, distinct from those required for airborne MBT trajectories.

Return JSON {"summary": "..."}.
